content: The proportion of total years of potential life lost (YPLL) due to homicide involving Black individuals in Michigan is 68%, significantly higher than the national average of 44%. Black homicide victims in Michigan are also slightly younger than White victims. In 1985, the average YPLL per homicide death was 33 years for Black individuals compared to 31 years for White individuals. Public health agencies must examine descriptive data like these to address homicide effectively. Additionally, analytic studies are needed to identify modifiable risk factors. Since 67% of Michigan's homicides in 1985 occurred in the Detroit area, these findings underscore the importance of implementing and evaluating prevention measures, such as Detroit's recently enacted handgun ordinance. At the state level, the high homicide rate has prompted plans to integrate health department and police databases for homicide surveillance. This integration may help identify factors contributing to the excess homicide rate in Michigan. Since the introduction of the measles vaccine in the United States in 1963, the reported incidence of measles has decreased by 99%, and indigenous measles transmission has been eliminated in most parts of the country. However, the goal of eliminating measles by October 1982 was not achieved. Between 1981 and 1987, annual reported cases ranged from a low of 1,497 in 1983 to a high of 6,282 in 1986. Large outbreaks have occurred among unvaccinated preschool-aged children in several inner-city areas. In these outbreaks, up to 88% of vaccine-eligible children aged 16 months to 4 years were unvaccinated, and as many as 40% of all cases occurred in children under 16 months of age. Surveys in outbreak areas revealed that only 49% to 65% of 2-year-olds had received the measles vaccine. Outbreaks have also occurred among school-aged children in schools with vaccination levels above 98%, with attack rates in individual schools ranging from 1% to 5%. Vaccine efficacy in these outbreaks has been high, but primary vaccine failure (2% to 10% of vaccinees who fail to seroconvert after vaccination) has played a significant role in transmission. Children vaccinated at 12 to 14 months of age have shown higher attack rates than those vaccinated at older ages. In some outbreaks, individuals vaccinated in the distant past, regardless of age at vaccination, have been at increased risk for disease. However, there is no conclusive evidence that waning vaccine-induced immunity is a major issue. The current measles elimination strategy involves administering a single dose of the measles vaccine at 15 months of age. A documented history of vaccination at or after 12 months of age is considered appropriate. High immunization levels, careful surveillance, and aggressive outbreak control are essential components of this strategy. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has periodically reviewed the strategy and progress toward measles elimination. At a recent meeting, the ACIP reviewed the epidemiology of measles in the United States and considered recommendations for modifying the elimination strategy. To increase vaccine coverage among preschool-aged children in inner-city areas, the ACIP emphasized the need for research to improve vaccine delivery. Proposed changes included a routine two-dose measles vaccination schedule and a one-time mass revaccination for school-aged children. Two new strategies were recommended: implementing a routine two-dose schedule in counties with recurrent measles transmission among preschool-aged children and lowering the age for routine vaccination to 9 months in areas with ongoing outbreaks. Infants vaccinated before their first birthday should receive a second dose at 15 months of age. Single-antigen measles vaccine should be used for infants under 1 year, while the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine should be used for those vaccinated at or after their first birthday. If resources do not permit a routine two-dose schedule, lowering the age for routine vaccination to 12 months is an acceptable alternative. Because individuals with primary vaccine failure play a prominent role in measles transmission, the ACIP recommends revaccination during outbreaks in secondary institutions such as high schools, colleges, and universities. In affected schools and those at risk, all students and their siblings vaccinated before 1980 should be revaccinated. This date was chosen because it captures most students vaccinated between 12 and 14 months of age, a group at increased risk of primary vaccine failure. The higher failure rate in this group may be due to suboptimal vaccine storage and handling or the greater instability of measles vaccines manufactured before 1979. If revaccination of all students vaccinated before 1980 is not feasible, targeting those vaccinated before 15 months of age is recommended. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Emory University will co-sponsor a course titled Epidemiology in Action, designed for state and local health department professionals. The course, scheduled for May 15–26, 1989, will focus on the practical application of epidemiology to public health problems and include lectures, workshops, classroom exercises, roundtable discussions, and an on-site community survey.
